extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of travel/nature essays; literary critics; aspiring descriptive writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and assessing travel/nature essays and portrayals of peoples and places—emphasizing fidelity of spirit, descriptive precision, choice of symbols, and modes of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of powerful, fitting symbols (the alchemist/gold)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all dreams, that of the alchemist is the most poetical, for he looked at the finest symbol. 'Gold... is the hidden light of the earth... being the last expression of vital energy.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose symbols that are deep, resonant, and apt (e.g., gold as 'hidden light' and final expression of vitality). Such symbols confer poetical weight; prefer symbols that synthesize natural and spiritual meaning rather than trivial or superficial emblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting by water makes scenes picturesque
rubrics_metrics.description: “All trades, all callings, become picturesque by the water's side, or on the water... The soil, the slovenliness, is washed out of every calling by its touch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use watery settings when you want to render ordinary life picturesque: water transforms mundane objects and occupations into pictorial, poetical subjects. If aiming for the picturesque, foreground the interaction of objects/people with water; anti-pattern: placing the same material on dry land without exploiting the water's visual/associative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and economy in dialect and action (sea-speech model)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Seamen must speak quick and bold, but also with utmost precision. They cannot reef and brace other than in a Homeric dialect,—therefore... there is a word for everything and every act, and a thing and an act for every word.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, forceful, and act-specific language for characters and technical scenes. Dialect and jargon that name acts precisely lend poetry and authenticity. Anti-pattern: long groping phrases or vague motions where a specific nautical term would be more vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's duty to create/augment beauty and omit dirt
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poet must be at the whole expense of the poetry... The poet must describe, as the painter sketches Irish peasant-girls and Danish fishwives, adding the beauty, and leaving out the dirt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing poetic description, the writer may (and should) select and enhance—add beauty and withhold extraneous squalor—to produce the intended aesthetic. Guidance: be deliberate about what to emphasize and what to omit to shape the reader's perception; anti-pattern: slavish, unedited transcription of every sordid detail that defeats poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersive, trustful observation of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nature always refuses to be seen by being stared at... But he who has gone to sleep in childish ease on her lap... will see all a mother's beauty in the look she bends upon him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To perceive nature fully, adopt an attitude of ease, familiarity, and trust rather than impertinent, exacting scrutiny. Long acquaintance and gentle attention reveal subtler beauties; anti-pattern: aggressive, surface-level observation that provokes nature's 'discharge' of expression and yields flat descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to the spirit of a scene over literal accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: On Catlin: “he is true to the spirit of the scene, and that a far better view can be got from him than from any source at present existing, of the Indian tribes... and of the country where their inheritance lay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging descriptive accounts, prioritize fidelity to the scene's animating spirit and overall truth of impression even when minute facts or exactitudes are imperfect. Good accounts convey the essential character and tone. Caveat: do not confuse spirit-faithfulness with deliberate fabrication of facts for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original phrasing and brevity in recorded oral narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Schoolcraft: had the mythological or hunting stories been 'written down exactly as they were received... the collection could not have been surpassed... the phraseology in which they were expressed has been entirely set aside, and the flimsy graces... substituted for the Spartan brevity and sinewy grasp of Indian speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transcribing oral lore or ethnographic speech, maintain the narrator's original wording, rhythm, and concision; avoid imposing florid literary 'graces' that dilute the original force. Anti-pattern: over-literaryizing oral material and replacing native diction with sentimental or fashionable phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid second-hand, academic, or stereotype portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: On Irving: “they have a stereotype, second-hand air. They lack the breath, the glow, the charming minute traits of living presence. His scenery is only fit to be glanced at from dioramic distance; his Indians are academic figures only.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for immediate, living detail and idiosyncratic traits rather than polished but lifeless, bookish representations. Inject 'minute traits of living presence' to prevent characters and scenes from reading as academic types or diorama pieces. Anti-pattern: relying on received clichés and polished generalities that obscure specific reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate facts to make a more pleasing story
rubrics_metrics.description: On Catlin: 'he is not to be depended on for the accuracy of his facts... he sometimes yields to the temptation of making out a story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain factual integrity in travel and ethnographic writing; avoid inventing or embellishing events purely to dramatize. If imaginative reconstruction is used, signal it to the reader. Anti-pattern: presenting invented incidents as observed fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even narrow or awkward accounts can convey key features
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most narrow-minded and awkward recital still bears some lineaments of the great features of this nature, and the races of men that illustrated them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating imperfect sources, look for essential 'lineaments'—those large, characteristic features that reveal truth despite clumsy form. Use such fragments as legitimate material for insight rather than dismissing them outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character depiction: portray inward qualities via demeanor and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of P.: 'He was thoroughly the gentleman, gentle because manly... his wise self-possession... patient shame... a religious submission... a fortitude... not the fortitude of the hero.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey a character's moral and psychological qualities through restrained, observable demeanor—posture, look, silence, the manner of bearing shame or courtesy—rather than via explicit declaration. Use small acts and composure to signal inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge towns/places by their function and social composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “There can be no two places in the world more completely thoroughfares than this place and Buffalo... To make the best provisions for the transmission of produce is their office... There are no provisions for the student or idler; to know what the place can give, you should be at work with the rest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or evaluating towns, attend to their practical role (e.g., transit/commerce) and how that shapes character. Avoid expecting cultural features inappropriate to the place's function; place-based criticism should account for role and population composition.
